title: The Tulane collection project: interviews and records
summary: Russell describes collecting interviews with musicians, wives and listeners, and phonograph records.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Hunting for old band photographs and scrapbooks

blocks.x: Well, Mr. Russell, what are you doing now at Tulane in this sort of research project towards preservation of jazz?

Well, it's strictly a collection project at present. We're collecting interviews, trying to preserve all that history of the old. The older the musicians, the better, of course, and other people, too, that happen to hear the music or maybe help promote it. In some cases, the wives and the daughters, sometimes the women know more about the history of it than the men, because maybe the husband went to work every night and played in one band, and the wife might have gotten around the different dances and heard different bands. Occasionally, they have a better memory, too. So it isn't just the musicians that we're interviewing.
But this, this, excuse me, go ahead.

Yes, but almost anyone who would remember some of the music back, oh, especially 40 to 60 years ago, those are the people we're trying to interview and collect the tape interviews. Also, we collect the phonograph records, which didn't come in until roughly 1917 on, especially through the 20s. So by that time, some of the music might have been sort of corrupted, some people might think, and we don't know, actually, because we don't have the old examples on record.
